points.en: EAI means explanation, application and illustration, developed for each division of the outline.
It is simple because the same procedure is repeated for every point and works for topical, textual and expository sermons.
The order of the three may vary, and each gets about equal attention.
Explaining the meaning of the text: drawing out what the Biblical writer was saying to his hearers.
Narration: giving the bare account of an event.
Description: painting a picture in words for the five senses.
For each form gives a sensible example of when it fits best.
Then: states what the passage said to its original hearers in their setting.
Universal: draws out the timeless principle that goes beyond that culture.
Now: gives a specific, concrete application for today that follows from the principle.
Uses a passage other than the storm-calming example given in the unit.
Research suggests that unless the speaker makes the application, the hearers will not make it.
Application is what relates Biblical truth to people's lives; without it the sermon is only a historical Bible study.
Gives two practical implications, such as speaking personally with 'we', in the present tense, and suggesting how to put it into practice.
Cites Spurgeon or Fosdick: application is where the sermon actually begins.
Names and describes at least four of the six sources: the Bible, observation, news, general reading and viewing, pastoral work, personal experience.
Gives a strength or a caution for the sources described, such as the Bible teaching while illustrating, or news making Scripture immediate.
Cautions: be discreet with examples about church members or family, and ask permission in pastoral stories.
Keyword method: a keyword organizes the subpoints under a division, just as a keyword links the main divisions.
Series of statements: no keyword is sought; rapid-fire statements provoke thought and word pictures.
Says when each suits, for example keyword when subpoints share a category, series of statements to stir thought and pictures.
Subpoints belong in the notes and are very rarely stated aloud.
Explanation: makes the meaning of the point from the text clear.
Application: relates the truth to the hearers' lives in a personal way.
Illustration: a story or image that throws light on the point.
The three parts are clearly labeled and given roughly equal attention.
Illustration is the servant: its job is to throw light on the truth and its application, never to be the point.
If it becomes master, the story overshadows the Biblical message and hearers remember the story but not the point.
Avoid it by choosing each illustration to serve a point, keeping it subordinate while still using one for every division.
Explanation: makes plain what the text means for the chosen point.
Application: the speaker states a concrete action the hearers should take, in the present.
Illustration: a story or image that throws light on the point.
The three parts are clearly labeled.
Names four of the six sources: the Bible, observation, news, general reading and viewing, pastoral work, personal experience.
For two of them gives one strength and one caution.
Bible: it teaches Scripture while illustrating, but the congregation may not realize it is an illustration.
Observation or pastoral work: be discreet about church members and family, and ask permission before sharing a story.
